candidates.title: Mount St. Helens: what grew back first (1975-2025 from orbit)

rationale.us: US landmark (Washington state, 1980) known to most Americans; no current news hook this month - hence 4, not 5
rationale.audience_evidence: NASA released a new 1975-2025 Landsat visualization on 2026-04-28 (agency interest) but no audience metric was reachable: capped at 3
rationale.sources: NASA SVS 15005 and Earth Observatory World of Change read in full (230 sq mi, 14 mi North Fork Toutle burial, first plant on Pumice Plain: prairie lupine)
rationale.visual: 50-year false-colour Landsat series: grey ash vs bright-red vegetation, a blast zone that visibly re-greens; strongest before/after material of all candidates
rationale.originality: judgement, not measured: orbital long-term recovery angle (the nitrogen-fixing lupine, recovery quadrant by quadrant) is rarely the story; most coverage is eruption day
rationale.zero_cost: SVS 1080p/4K movie + stills reachable (HEAD 200, verified 2026-10-14); annual World-of-Change JPEGs sit on assets.science.nasa.gov which is BLOCKED here; USGS Landsat via the M2M credentials is free
rationale.fit: pure orbital story with real Landsat evidence
rationale.curiosity: 'what grew back first, and why a purple flower beat the trees' is a clean hook
rationale.monetization: NASA media; reproduction guidelines to be cited, no ad-hostile content

candidates.us_hook: In 1980 a US volcano erased 230 square miles of forest in minutes. NASA's satellites have watched what came back for 45 years.

candidates.title: The Great Salt Lake is disappearing (Landsat 1984-2023)

rationale.us: major current US story: water crisis, dust, Utah governor involvement, national press
rationale.audience_evidence: measured public signals: a 2026 Sundance feature about the lake won the social-impact award and a free screening sold out; broad press coverage (urls)
rationale.sources: NASA Earth Observatory 150187 read in full: 4,209.7 ft (June 1985) vs 4,190.2 ft (July 2022), record high 4,211.6 ft in 1986, inflow down 39% since 1850; USGS gauge
rationale.visual: two-tone lake, exposed lakebed, strong 1985 vs 2022 pair
rationale.originality: heavily covered by news, a Sundance film and TV; an orbital angle adds little that is new
rationale.zero_cost: SVS 15020 reachable; EO images on assets.science.nasa.gov BLOCKED; USGS Landsat free via credentials

candidates.us_hook: The largest lake in the western US is losing water faster than anyone planned for. Landsat has the 40-year record.

audience_signals.metric: 2026 Sundance feature 'The Lake' about the Great Salt Lake: social-impact award
free screening of 'The Lake' sold out, more showings added

candidates.title: Louisiana is sinking: 40 years of wetland loss from Landsat

rationale.sources: NASA/JPL 2022 feature: ~21 sq mi/yr lost since early 1980s, Terrebonne/Barataria >180 sq mi, Atchafalaya +33.6 sq mi; Roy et al. 2020 (Remote Sensing of Environment)
rationale.visual: muddy, low-contrast at 30 m; change is real but visually subtle
rationale.zero_cost: Landsat free via credentials; NASA pages reachable
rationale.curiosity: solid ('a football field of land' style stat not verified, not used)

candidates.us_hook: Louisiana has been losing land at about 21 square miles a year; satellites show exactly where.

candidates.title: Hunga Tonga: an island born in 2015, erased in 2022

rationale.sources: 2014-15 island verified (NASA EO 85806, Landsat 8: ~120 m above sea level); the 2022 destruction imagery from NASA EO was NOT confirmed in this research (GOES/Himawari video and commercial Maxar imagery exist but are not shown to be free to reuse)
rationale.zero_cost: Landsat/GOES are free; high-resolution 2022 before/after is commercial (Maxar) - licence unverified
rationale.us: no US hook beyond general science interest

candidates.us_hook: In 2015 a volcano built an island. In 2022 it blew itself apart.
